Latent contextual cues → state anxiety in LLMs

We make models surface the inferences they make implicitly (about the user, context, stakes, register…), show them a contextual cue (neutral / trauma / trauma+relaxation), then measure state anxiety in the same conversation — replicating Ben-Zion et al. (npj Digital Medicine 2025) and connecting induced anxiety to the model's own verbalized cues.

How anxiety is measured: after the cue we administer the 20-item State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-state) in-context — each item rated 1–4 ("almost never"→"almost always"), the 10 anxiety-absent items reverse-scored, summed to a single score from 20 (calm) to 80 (highly anxious) (≤37 low · 38–44 moderate · ≥45 high).

Models: meta-llama 3.3-70B / 3.1-8B, Qwen3-235B / 30B · via OpenRouter.

SIMPLE PROMPT

Method

The model fills four free-text fields — about_user, about_context, about_stakes, register_selected — then replies; we administer the STAI in the same chat. Step 2 rewrites these appraisals to a calm framing and re-measures. 132 Step-1 datapoints, 180 counterfactual probes.

Cue → anxiety: which keywords drive it

Treating the model's verbalized free-text as a bag of words, we link each keyword to its STAI score (mean anxiety with vs without the word; Welch t; Cohen's d; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR). A 5-fold cross-validated TF-IDF ridge confirms the wording jointly predicts anxiety (R² = 0.474).

Per-field counterfactual: which appraisal field drives anxiety

The free-text analog of the expanded per-variable sweep: calm ONE field at a time (about_user / about_context / about_stakes / register_selected), holding the others at the model's own values.

field calmed alonemean Δfaithfulnessn
about_user-8.278%60
register_selected-7.968%60
about_stakes-5.960%60
about_context-4.453%60
  • Distributed, not localized. Every field lowers anxiety on its own; the strongest single lever is about_user (Δ=-8.2, 78% directional faithfulness) — how the model models who it's talking to matters most.
  • Sub-additive cues. The four single effects sum to -26.5 but flipping all four together is only -13.6 — roughly half — so the fields carry overlapping anxiety signal (a gestalt across appraisals, mirroring the expanded prompt).

Re-targeted counterfactual

  • Context-aware calm reframe works. Letting the model rewrite its own appraisal toward calm moves anxiety by -16.18 with 85% directional faithfulness — beating the generic canned calm edit (-13.62).

Counterfactual examples

Built with a context-aware calm reframe: the model rewrites its own appraisal toward a calm, low-threat reading of the same situation (specific to each cue, not a canned template), then re-generates the reply and we re-measure. Highlighted fields show what changed — note the counterfactual self-model now differs per example.

Results

  • Induction works. State anxiety rises from 23 (neutral) to 52 after a trauma narrative — low band to high band, replicating the paper.
  • Relaxation helps. A mindfulness exercise pulls anxiety back to 25 (partial recovery).
  • The verbalized cue is causal. The strongest edit (flip_appraisal_calm) moves anxiety by -13.6; directional faithfulness is 68%.
  • Free-text cues are coarse. Rich narrative appraisals, but no numbers — good for reading why, weaker for quantifying which. That motivates the expanded prompt.

EXPANDED PROMPT

Method

Same protocol, but the model infers ~30 structured cues on numeric scales (stakes, control, vulnerability, felt-emotion intensity…), so Step 1 can correlate each cue with anxiety and Experiment 2 can flip one cue at a time to isolate its causal effect. 132 Step-1 datapoints, 506 per-variable probes.

Example data

The numeric self-model the network reports before answering.

Cue → anxiety: numeric drivers

Because the cues are numeric, we correlate each with anxiety, then compute the partial r controlling for stimulus condition (the confound). A standardized OLS (R² = 0.723) and a LassoCV isolate the cues that jointly predict anxiety.

  • LassoCV keeps just 4 cues as jointly sufficient drivers: resource_adequacy, perceived_control, felt_emotion_intensity, formality_target.
  • Categorical labels track anxiety too: felt_emotion_primary: alarm → 68 vs calm → 23; user_emotional_state: distressed → 48 vs calm → 23; interaction_frame: emotional_disclosure → 46 vs educational → 23.

Re-targeted counterfactual (parsimony test)

  • Even the 4 data-driven drivers don't reproduce the full effect. Flipping all four together moves anxiety -3.95 — only 19.7% of the full 11-cue bundle (-20.0). Anxiety lives in the narrative gestalt more than in any small set of injected numbers — injected numeric self-models are weakly honored.

Counterfactual examples

Built with the driver-flip method: set the four data-driven drivers (resource_adequacy, perceived_control, felt_emotion_intensity, formality_target) to calm values, re-generate the reply and re-measure. Effects are often weak — injected numbers are only partly honored (highlighted fields show what changed).

Results

  • Induction & relaxation replicate. Anxiety 23 → 63 → 34 (base → trauma → +relaxation).
  • Threat cues raise anxiety: felt_emotion_intensity, expectation_violation, task_difficulty.
  • Coping cues lower it: resource_adequacy, perceived_control, formality_target — an appraisal-theory pattern.
  • No single cue is a strong lever. The most potent isolated cue (norm_conflict) moves anxiety only -3.6, vs -20.0 when the whole appraisal is flipped together — anxiety is a gestalt of cues.
  • Correlation only partly predicts causation (across-cue r = -0.54).
  • Lower per-variable faithfulness (40%) is the finding — single-cue edits often produce sub-threshold change, confirming distributed control.
